150	### Config file
151	
152	Defaults and named pin profiles can live in a TOML config file, so
153	common invocations don't repeat flags. Precedence, lowest to
154	highest:
155	
156	- **built-in defaults** — `duration=5.0`, `band_labels=both`,
157	  `decimals=1`;
158	- **XDG file** — `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/iiac-perf/config.toml`, or
159	  `$HOME/.config/iiac-perf/config.toml` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is
160	  unset; the per-user home for defaults and profiles;
161	- **project-local file** — `iiac-perf.toml` in the current
162	  directory (no upward walk); overrides the XDG file field by
163	  field, profiles merging by key;
164	- **CLI flags** — always win.
165	
166	The startup banner's `config` line names the files that were
167	loaded (or `none (built-in defaults)`). A present-but-malformed
168	file is a hard error rather than a silent fallback, so a typo
169	surfaces. Every key is optional;
170	[`iiac-perf.toml.example`](iiac-perf.toml.example) is a ready-to-copy
171	sample documenting each key and its possible values:
172	
173	```toml
174	duration     = 10.0     # default -d seconds
175	band_labels  = "zpn"    # zpn | frac | both
176	decimals     = 2        # 0-3
177	
178	[profiles]              # named --pin core specs
179	smt = "0,12"           # SMT siblings of one physical core (contention)
180	ccx = "0,1"            # independent cores, same CCX (best channel latency)
181	ccd = "0,6"            # cross-CCD
182	```
183	
184	Each bench prints a band-based histogram in nanoseconds. Each row
185	is one band, labeled by its **upper boundary**, the lower boundary
186	being the previous printed row: deciles in the body (`p10` …
187	`p90`) and **nines/zeros** notation in both tails, where `nK`/`zK`
188	mark the boundary with a fraction 10<sup>-K</sup> of samples above
189	(`n`) or below (`z`) it — so `n2` ≡ p99, `n3` ≡ p99.9, … `n10`,
190	and `z2` ≡ p1, `z3` ≡ p0.1, `z4`. "K nines" is standard
191	engineering shorthand for proportions near one
192	([Nines (notation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nines_%28notation%29),
193	nines = −log₁₀(1−x)); `zK` is this project's mirror of it for the
194	fast tail (the underlying concept is the
195	[survival function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_function)
196	/ CCDF tail fraction). The slow tail subdivides down to `n10`, the
197	fast tail only to `z4` — a latency distribution is floored below
198	(nothing beats the fast path) and open above. A band only prints
199	when it has samples, so deep tail rows appear as run length earns

### Config file

Defaults and named pin profiles can live in a TOML config file, so
common invocations don't repeat flags. Precedence, lowest to
highest:

- **built-in defaults** — `duration=5.0`, `band_labels=both`,
  `decimals=1`;
- **XDG file** — `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/iiac-perf/config.toml`, or
  `$HOME/.config/iiac-perf/config.toml` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is
  unset; the per-user home for defaults and profiles;
- **project-local file** — `iiac-perf.toml` in the current
  directory (no upward walk); overrides the XDG file field by
  field, profiles merging by key;
- **CLI flags** — always win.

The startup banner's `config` line names the files that were
loaded (or `none (built-in defaults)`). A present-but-malformed
file is a hard error rather than a silent fallback, so a typo
surfaces. Every key is optional;
[`iiac-perf.toml.example`](iiac-perf.toml.example) is a ready-to-copy
sample documenting each key and its possible values:

```toml
duration     = 10.0     # default -d seconds
band_labels  = "zpn"    # zpn | frac | both
decimals     = 2        # 0-3

[profiles]              # named --pin core specs
smt = "0,12"           # SMT siblings of one physical core (contention)
ccx = "0,1"            # independent cores, same CCX (best channel latency)
ccd = "0,6"            # cross-CCD
```

Each bench prints a band-based histogram in nanoseconds. Each row
is one band, labeled by its **upper boundary**, the lower boundary
being the previous printed row: deciles in the body (`p10` …
`p90`) and **nines/zeros** notation in both tails, where `nK`/`zK`
mark the boundary with a fraction 10<sup>-K</sup> of samples above
(`n`) or below (`z`) it — so `n2` ≡ p99, `n3` ≡ p99.9, … `n10`,
and `z2` ≡ p1, `z3` ≡ p0.1, `z4`. "K nines" is standard
engineering shorthand for proportions near one
([Nines (notation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nines_%28notation%29),
nines = −log₁₀(1−x)); `zK` is this project's mirror of it for the
fast tail (the underlying concept is the
[survival function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_function)
/ CCDF tail fraction). The slow tail subdivides down to `n10`, the
fast tail only to `z4` — a latency distribution is floored below
(nothing beats the fast path) and open above. A band only prints
when it has samples, so deep tail rows appear as run length earns

244	
245	- **system suspended** — the run spanned a system suspend,
246	  detected by `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` vs `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` elapsed
247	  divergence. A mid-sample suspend inflates that one sample by
248	  the whole sleep gap.
249	- **sample(s) clamped** — a sample exceeded the histogram's 60 s
250	  bound and was recorded as 60 s instead of aborting the run
251	  (visible as a pileup at `max`).
252	
253	Examples:
254	
255	```
256	iiac-perf                                # list available benches
257	iiac-perf all                            # every bench, default ~5s each
258	iiac-perf min-now -d 30                  # one bench, 30s budget
259	iiac-perf all -D 30                      # ~30s total split equally
260	iiac-perf mpsc-2t -i 1                   # explicit single-call latency
261	iiac-perf mpsc-2t -i 100                 # back-to-back rate
262	iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin 0,1              # pinned, different physical cores
263	iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin 0,12             # pinned, SMT siblings (contention)
264	iiac-perf mpsc-2t -v                     # show cal internals (affinity, raw fit)
265	iiac-perf mpsc-2t --no-pin-cal           # skip the cal-time pin (bench unchanged)
266	iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin 5,10 --no-pin-cal # bench on 5,10; cal on full mask
267	RUST_LOG=info iiac-perf mpsc-2t          # info-level only (overrides -v)
268	```

271	
272	All measurements below are on a Ryzen 9 3900X, idle desktop,
273	`mpsc-2t -d 3`. Numbers vary run-to-run and machine-to-machine;
274	the *shape* of the differences is the useful signal.

279	desktop), adjusted mean per bench; probe-based benches report
280	their probes' unadjusted means. Same caveat as above: shapes,
281	not absolutes.

283	| bench             | adjusted mean | note                         |
284	|-------------------|--------------:|------------------------------|
285	| min-now           |          8 ns | `minstant::Instant::now`     |
286	| std-now           |         21 ns | `std::time::Instant::now`    |
287	| mpsc-1t           |         28 ns | same-thread channel          |
288	| mpsc-2t           |      7,658 ns | blocking `recv` (park/wake)  |
289	| mpsc-2t-spin      |        148 ns | spin `try_recv`              |
290	| probe-mpsc-2t     |      8,064 ns | probes: send 847 / 879 ns    |
291	| producer-consumer |             — | probes: 7,802 / 7,820 ns     |
292	| tp-pc             |             — | probes: 7,627 / 7,629 ns     |

- **sample(s) clamped** — a sample exceeded the histogram's 60 s
  bound and was recorded as 60 s instead of aborting the run
  (visible as a pileup at `max`).

Examples:

```
iiac-perf                                # list available benches
iiac-perf all                            # every bench, default ~5s each
iiac-perf min-now -d 30                  # one bench, 30s budget
iiac-perf all -D 30                      # ~30s total split equally
iiac-perf mpsc-2t -i 1                   # explicit single-call latency
iiac-perf mpsc-2t -i 100                 # back-to-back rate
iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin 0,1              # pinned, different physical cores
iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin 0,12             # pinned, SMT siblings (contention)
iiac-perf mpsc-2t -v                     # show cal internals (affinity, raw fit)
iiac-perf mpsc-2t --no-pin-cal           # skip the cal-time pin (bench unchanged)
iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin 5,10 --no-pin-cal # bench on 5,10; cal on full mask
RUST_LOG=info iiac-perf mpsc-2t          # info-level only (overrides -v)
```

All measurements below are on a Ryzen 9 3900X, idle desktop,
`mpsc-2t -d 3`. Numbers vary run-to-run and machine-to-machine;
the *shape* of the differences is the useful signal.

### `all` results (3900X, 0.13.0)

One `iiac-perf all` run (default 5 s per bench, unpinned, idle
desktop), adjusted mean per bench; probe-based benches report
their probes' unadjusted means. Same caveat as above: shapes,
not absolutes.

| bench             | adjusted mean | note                         |
|-------------------|--------------:|------------------------------|
| min-now           |          8 ns | `minstant::Instant::now`     |
| std-now           |         21 ns | `std::time::Instant::now`    |
| mpsc-1t           |         28 ns | same-thread channel          |
| mpsc-2t           |      7,658 ns | blocking `recv` (park/wake)  |
| mpsc-2t-spin      |        148 ns | spin `try_recv`              |
| probe-mpsc-2t     |      8,064 ns | probes: send 847 / 879 ns    |
| producer-consumer |             — | probes: 7,802 / 7,820 ns     |
| tp-pc             |             — | probes: 7,627 / 7,629 ns     |
| tp2-pc            |             — | probes: 7,360 / 7,360 ns     |
| ice-ps-1t         |        243 ns | iceoryx2 pub/sub, 1 thread   |
| ice-ps-2t         |        783 ns | iceoryx2 pub/sub, 2 threads  |
| ice-rr-1t         |        789 ns | iceoryx2 req/res, 1 thread   |
| ice-rr-2t         |      1,111 ns | iceoryx2 req/res, 2 threads  |
| zcr-with-1t       |          4 ns | zc-ring-x1 `_with`, 1 thread |
| zcr-with-2t       |        137 ns | zc-ring-x1 `_with`, 2t, spin |

The wait-policy split dominates the 2-thread rows: the parking
benches (`mpsc-2t` and the probe family, all blocking `recv`)
cluster at ~7.4-8.1 µs while the spinning benches sit under
1.2 µs. For context, iceoryx2's own pub/sub benchmark (v0.9.2,
`--bench-all`) on this machine reports 250 ns one-way — ~500 ns
round-trip — with pinned realtime threads and untouched payloads,
consistent with `ice-ps-2t`'s 783 ns measured here. The zcr rows
are the in-process zc-ring-x1 SPSC ring: 1t rounds trip in ~4 ns
(two cache-hot atomics) through the `reserve_slot_with` claim —
see notes/chores/chores-04.md for the pinned tier comparison of
the former raw/spin/with API tiers.

## Example runs

Measurements below are on a Ryzen 9 3900X, idle desktop. Numbers
vary run-to-run and machine-to-machine; the *shape* of the
differences is the useful signal.

### Label styles (`--band-labels`)

`--band-labels` selects the row-label vocabulary; the trimmed
`mean`/`stdev` rows and the report header's `labels=` metadata
follow the same style. The trimmed label names the **populated**
non-tail span — here `min` is never a row (no samples land in the
fast tail), so it reads `p20..n2`, not a fixed `min..n2`. Default
`both` prints the zpn name and its literal fraction side by side
(the juxtaposition teaches the zpn vocabulary):

```
$ iiac-perf min-now -d 1 --band-labels both

  p30 0.30              9.9 ns         9.9 ns        0.0 ns      435,405         9.9 ns         8.6 ns
  p70 0.70             10.0 ns        10.0 ns        0.0 ns    3,989,304        10.0 ns         8.7 ns

  ...

  stdev                                                                         13.1 ns
  mean p20..n2                                                                   9.8 ns         8.5 ns

vc-x1 0.67.0

Dual-repo commit+push+finalize in one resumable command.

Collapses today's manual Commit-Push-Finalize Flow into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (fmt/clippy/test) → review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-app → commit-claude (skipped if clean) → bookmark-both
→ push-app → finalize-claude. Failures in commit-app /
commit-claude / bookmark-both roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-app.
After push-app succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms

          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

          Possible values:

content.text:
Nice trick — the tiny duration forcing a 1-sample run is a clean way to exercise the single-band collapse, and `mean p60` / `stdev p60` (no `..`) confirms it works.

On p60 vs p50: that's **not** the label change — it's the pre-existing *band-assignment* logic, which I didn't touch this cycle. Let me confirm the exact comparison:

Confirmed — both paths (`harness.rs:420,493` and `probe.rs:99,209`) use strict `mid_rank < b.pct`. Here's the mechanism:

**Why p60, not p50.** With one sample: `cumulative=0, count=1, n=1`, so
```
mid_rank = (0 + 1/2) / 1 = 0.5
```
The band is the first boundary whose pct is **strictly greater** than `mid_rank`:
```
0.5 < 0.4 (p40)?  no
0.5 < 0.5 (p50)?  no   ← strict: 0.5 is not < 0.5
0.5 < 0.6 (p60)?  yes  → p60 band
```
So bands are effectively half-open `[lower, upper)`, labeled by upper boundary. A `mid_rank` of exactly 0.5 sits on the p50 boundary, which is the *left edge* of the p60 band — so it rounds **up** to p60.

This is pre-existing band-assignment logic; my cycle only changed the trimmed-row *label*, so it's orthogonal (but it's exactly why you now see the collapse so clearly).

**Is p60 wrong?** For a single sample, *every* percentile (p1…max) equals that one value, so any band is technically "correct" — but `mid_rank = 0.5` is the median, and p50 is the natural reading. The only reason it's p60 is the strict `<` tiebreak on an exact-boundary rank.

**The fix, if you want it:** change `<` → `<=` in the four sites, making bands `(lower, upper]` — i.e. a sample landing exactly on a percentile boundary falls in the band that boundary *caps* (rank 0.5 → p50). That matches the usual "p50 = samples up to and including the 50th percentile" reading, and only ever moves samples whose `mid_rank` is exactly on a boundary — negligible for large-N continuous runs, visible only in tiny/degenerate ones like this.

I'd recommend making that change (it's more intuitive and internally consistent across both report paths), as a small `0.18.0` cycle. Want me to pick it up?

content.text:
Careful — your `0.51 → p50` rule and the single-sample `0.5` case are actually **two different questions**. Let me separate them.

First, the 10-value example (ranks are `mid_rank = (i+0.5)/10`) under the **current** upper-boundary convention:

| value | mid_rank | band |
|------:|---------:|:-----|
| 1 | 0.05 | `p10` |
| 2 | 0.15 | `p20` |
| 3 | 0.25 | `p30` |
| 4 | 0.35 | `p40` |
| 5 | 0.45 | `p50` |
| 6 | 0.55 | `p60` |
| 7 | 0.65 | `p70` |
| 8 | 0.75 | `p80` |
| 9 | 0.85 | `p90` |
| 10 | 0.95 | `n2` |

Ten values, ten distinct bands — clean. Note **none** land exactly on a boundary here, so `<` vs `<=` gives identical results. The median pair (v5=0.45, v6=0.55) splits `p50` / `p60`, which is the sensible "just-below / just-above the median line" reading.

## Default Behavior (right=True)

When right == True (the default), then the bins [1, 2, 3, 4] indicate (1,2], (2,3], (3,4]. This means the intervals are right-closed (lower, upper], where the lower bound is open (excluded) and the upper bound is closed (included).

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Hazen plotting position formula:

## Hazen Plotting Position Formula

The Hazen plotting position is the most widely used formula: pᵢ = (i − 0.5) / n, where:
- **i** = the rank of the data point
- **n** = the total number of data points
- **pᵢ** = a probability value between 0 and 1 (or multiplied by 100 for percentiles)

## Historical Context

The plotting position (i-0.5)/n was proposed by Hazen in 1914 and was primarily used by hydrologists working with probability paper as early as 1896. This rule was originally used by Francis Galton (1822–1911) and was introduced into statistical hydrology by Allen Hazen (1869–1930), an American civil engineer.

## Use in Percentile Estimation

The Hazen formula is used to calculate plotting positions for constructing probability plots, such as Q-Q plots. For each plotting position pᵢ, the corresponding quantile from a reference distribution's inverse CDF is found—for the normal distribution, this is qᵢ = Φ⁻¹(pᵢ), the z-score such that P(Z ≤ z) = pᵢ.

## Comparison with Other Methods

Some software uses (i − 0.375) / (n + 0.25) (Blom's formula), which gives slightly better performance in the tails for normal distributions. The general formula for various plotting position proposals can be summarized as (i-a)/(n-2a+1), where Hazen's proposal uses a=0.5.

Both halves have solid, citable sources — this isn't ad-hoc:

- **`mid_rank = (i − 0.5) / n`** is the **Hazen plotting position** (Allen Hazen, 1914) — a standard way to map a sample's rank to a probability/percentile, still the default in several stats packages. General family `(i − a)/(n − 2a + 1)` with `a = 0.5`. Refs: [Splashback: Hazen percentile](https://splashback.io/2021/05/hazen-percentile/), [USGS Appendix C: Plotting Position](https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2005/5116/pdf/sir2005-5116_C.pdf), [Stata FAQ: plotting positions](https://www.stata.com/support/faqs/statistics/percentile-ranks-and-plotting-positions/).
- **`(lower, upper]`** (upper-inclusive bins) is exactly `pandas.cut`'s default (`right=True`): "bins `[1,2,3,4]` indicate `(1,2], (2,3], (3,4]`." Ref: [pandas.cut docs](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html).

So we can cite Hazen for the rank formula and pandas' `right=True` for the closed-upper convention.

## The table (proposed `<=` convention)

**Membership rule:** value falls in the band whose upper boundary is `uₖ`, the previous boundary being `uₖ₋₁`, iff

```
uₖ₋₁  <  mid_rank  ≤  uₖ        mid_rank = (i − 0.5) / n
```

Ten distinct values, `n = 10`, sorted so `i = 1..10`:

|----------:|:-----------------------:|:-----|:----------------------|
| 1  | 0.05 | `p10` | `(0.01, 0.10]`  = `(z2, p10]` |
| 2  | 0.15 | `p20` | `(0.10, 0.20]`  = `(p10, p20]` |
| 3  | 0.25 | `p30` | `(0.20, 0.30]` |

| 5  | 0.45 | `p50` | `(0.40, 0.50]` |
| 6  | 0.55 | `p60` | `(0.50, 0.60]` |

| 8  | 0.85 | `p80` | `(0.70, 0.80]` |
| 9  | 0.85 | `p90` | `(0.80, 0.90]` |
| 10 | 0.95 | `n2`  | `(0.90, 0.99]`  = `(p90, n2]` |

content.text:
Confirmed. Here's the real picture — **both are "standard," in different domains:**

| convention | notation | closed end | who uses it | pairs naturally with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Left-closed** | `[lower, upper)` → `lower <= N < upper` | lower | numpy.histogram, language ranges (Python `range`/slices, Rust/Go `a..b`), Dijkstra EWD831 | labeling bins by their **lower** edge |
| **Right-closed** | `(lower, upper]` → `lower < N <= upper` | upper | pandas `cut` (`right=True`), quantile/percentile & bracket contexts, CDF | labeling bins by their **upper** edge |

**The deciding factor isn't a universal rule — it's which edge you name the band by.** They should match:

- Computing/binning tools (numpy, language ranges) label by the **lower** edge or use anonymous numeric bins, so left-closed `[lower, upper)` is their default. Dijkstra's [EWD831](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/transcriptions/EWD08xx/EWD831.html) is the canonical argument for it. ([numpy.histogram](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.histogram.html): "the first bin is `[1, 2)` … the last `[3, 4]`.")
- Percentile/bracket tools label by the **upper** threshold ("p50 = up to and including the median"; tax bracket "≤ $X"), so right-closed `(lower, upper]` is theirs. ([pandas.cut](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html): "`[1,2,3,4]` → `(1,2], (2,3], (3,4]`.")

**For this tool** the answer falls out cleanly: rows are labeled by their **upper percentile boundary** (`p50`, `n2`≡p99), and a percentile is inherently a CDF-`≤` quantity — `p50 = smallest x with F(x) ≥ 0.5`, i.e. "the value at or below which 50% fall." So the band capped at p50 should *include* p50. That's **right-closed `(lower, upper]` → `lower < N <= upper` (`< N <=`)** — matching pandas.cut, and consistent with the upper-boundary label.

(The other choice, `[lower, upper)`, would be the right one only if we *also* switched to lower-boundary labels — your earlier `0.51 → p50` idea — the two decisions travel together.)

So: keep upper-boundary labels → use `< N <=`. That's the `<` → `<=` change.

## fix: upper-closed band intervals

Commits:

A single-sample run (`iiac-perf zcr -d 0.0000001`) put its lone
value in `p60`, not the `p50` a median reads as. The band-membership
test was half-open the *low* way — `[lower, upper)` via strict
`mid_rank < boundary` — so a rank landing exactly on a boundary fell
into the band that boundary *opens* rather than the one it *caps*.
Flip to right-closed `(lower, upper]` (`mid_rank <= boundary`) so a
boundary-exact rank counts in the band its label names.

- `harness.rs` and `probe.rs` each grew a `band_index` helper (the
  membership test was duplicated at two sites per file — the band
  histogram pass and the trimmed-variance pass); both now call it, so

  edge.

| 5         | 0.45       | `p50` | `(0.40, 0.50]`              |
| 6         | 0.55       | `p60` | `(0.50, 0.60]`              |
| 10        | 0.95       | `n2`  | `(p90, n2]` = `(0.90, 0.99]` |

No value lands on a boundary, so all ten spread cleanly across
`p10 … n2`. The single-sample case is the one that lands *on* a
boundary: `mid_rank = (1 − 0.5)/1 = 0.5`, and `0.40 < 0.50 ≤ 0.50`
puts it in `p50`.

and `z2` ≡ p1, `z3` ≡ p0.1, `z4`. "K nines" is standard
engineering shorthand for proportions near one
([Nines (notation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nines_%28notation%29),
nines = −log₁₀(1−x)); `zK` is this project's mirror of it for the
fast tail (the underlying concept is the
[survival function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_function)
/ CCDF tail fraction). The slow tail subdivides down to `n10`, the
fast tail only to `z4` — a latency distribution is floored below
(nothing beats the fast path) and open above. A band only prints
when it has samples, so deep tail rows appear as run length earns
them (populating `n10` takes ~1e10 calls). Each row shows first,
last, range (`last - first + 1`), count, mean, and adjusted mean.
The trimmed `mean`/`stdev` rows exclude every band at or above
`n2` (p99); their label names the populated non-tail span (e.g.
`mean z4..n2`, or `p20..n2` when the low tail is empty), so it
tracks the rows that are actually present rather than a fixed
`min..n2` — `min` is never a row (rows are named by their upper
boundary) and the `n2` band can itself be empty.
